summary: EAP Re-authentication Protocol extensions let a peer re-authenticate efficiently with another authenticator, without repeating the full EAP exchange, using an EAP re-authentication server.

eli5.summary: Instead of showing all your papers again every time you walk into a new room, you carry a quick pass.

questions: what is the eap re-authentication protocol
how to re-authenticate with eap without a full exchange
how does eap re-authentication protocol work
what is the difference between rrk and rik
subtitle: A one-round-trip way to re-authenticate with EAP when moving between access points, without repeating the full login.

tldr.problem: When a device moves to a new authenticator, repeating the full EAP exchange can take several round trips and slow the handover. Method-specific shortcuts take at least 2 round trips in most cases, and some methods have none.
tldr.mechanism: ERP derives re-authentication keys from the key material of the first full EAP run. The peer then proves it holds one of them in a single EAP-Initiate/Re-auth and EAP-Finish/Re-auth exchange with an ER server, which hands a fresh per-authenticator key to the authenticator.
tldr.outcome: Re-authentication works with any EAP method and can be served by a local ER server. This RFC is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5296 and is backward compatible with it.

today: RFC 6696 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5296, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the metadata for this unit. It remains the definition of ERP for this site.

sections.title: Why Re-authenticate Faster
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is mainly used for network access authentication. A peer and an EAP server authenticate each other through an authenticator, and the server sends the authenticator a Master Session Key (MSK) that is used to set up the keys for the link.

When a peer moves to another authenticator, a full EAP exchange with another run of the EAP method can take several round trips and increase handover time. Some methods keep state to speed up re-authentication, but this takes at least 2 round trips with the original EAP server in most cases, and several methods offer no support at all. Sharing keys across authenticators is another shortcut, but then the compromise of one authenticator compromises key material established via others.

The RFC therefore asks for a method-independent protocol that completes in fewer than 2 round trips, preferably with a local server. The result is the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP), built from the EAP Re-authentication Extensions (ERXs).

RFC 6696 obsoletes RFC 5296 and is fully backward compatible with it. Main changes: the home ER server no longer has to be co-located with the EAP server, bootstrapping behavior is clarified, and the authenticator is now recommended to start the exchange with an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message.
sections.eli5: Walking into every new building and showing your whole ID takes ages. ERP lets you show a short pass that proves you already showed your ID once.

sections.title: How ERP Works
sections.content:
ERP defines three roles. The ER peer is the device. The ER authenticator passes messages along, much as an EAP authenticator does. The ER server does the server side of ERP; it may be in the home domain or in the local (visited) domain, and it need not be part of a full EAP server.

The first time a peer attaches, it does a full EAP exchange. Both sides derive an EMSK from it, and from that a re-authentication root key (rRK) and a re-authentication integrity key (rIK). These stay on the peer and the ER server and are never handed to anyone else.

Later, ERP is a single round-trip exchange. The authenticator may send EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start. The peer sends EAP-Initiate/Re-auth, integrity protected with the rIK. The server checks proof of possession and freshness, derives an rMSK and answers with EAP-Finish/Re-auth. The rMSK travels to the authenticator in the AAA message, in the way the MSK travels with EAP-Success. Both sides can then start the lower-layer security association.

If the authenticator does not support ERP, it silently discards the Re-auth message because the EAP code is greater than 4, and the peer falls back to normal EAP. The authenticator may wait a short, locally configured time after the Start message and then send an EAP-Request/Identity.
sections.eli5: After the first full check, you and the school office share a secret handshake. At each new classroom you do the handshake once, and the office tells the teacher you are fine.

sections.title: Home and Local ER Servers
sections.content:
ERP can run with an ER server in the home domain or in a local domain. If the peer is at home, or no local server exists, the peer should do an ERP bootstrap exchange with the home ER server to obtain the domain name.

With a local ER server, the peer learns the local domain name from a lower-layer advertisement or from an ERP exchange. The local server gets a Domain-Specific Root Key (DSRK) from the home EAP server, along with the key name EMSKname, usually by asking during the first EAP exchange. The peer derives the same domain-specific keys from the EMSK and the domain name. Both sides keep a sequence number, starting at zero, for the specific keyName-NAI.

The keyName-NAI names the key in use. Its username part is the EMSKname and its realm is the domain name of the ER server, so the authenticator knows where to send each message.
sections.eli5: The key can be checked either by the head office far away or by a branch office next door. The branch is quicker, so the peer uses it when there is one.

sections.title: The ER Key Hierarchy
sections.content:
Each re-authentication gives the peer and the authenticator an rMSK, which serves the same purposes as an MSK from a full EAP run. The keys form a small tree, with the rRK at the top.

  • rRK is derived from the EMSK or a DSRK using the KDF from RFC 5295. It is used only as a root for re-authentication, never to protect data, and MUST NOT leave the peer and the server.
  • rIK is derived from the rRK and is used to integrity protect ERP messages as proof of possession. It MUST NOT be used to derive any other keys and also stays on the peer and the server. The cryptosuite and length are part of the derivation, so differently sized rIKs are cryptographically separate.
  • rMSK is derived from the rRK using the 16-bit sequence number as input, and is delivered to the authenticator. A given rMSK MUST NOT be shared by multiple authenticators.

A child key's lifetime never exceeds its parent's. When the parent key expires, the rRK and rIK MUST be removed from use. Each key is bound to its purpose by a label, such as EAP Re-authentication Root Key@ietf.org for the rRK.
sections.eli5: One master key makes a few helper keys. One helper proves who you are, and a new throwaway key is made for each room you enter, so one stolen room key does not open the others.

sections.title: Bootstrapping, Replay Protection and Failures
sections.content:
Bootstrapping comes in two kinds. In implicit bootstrapping, the local server asks for a DSRK during the initial EAP exchange. In explicit bootstrapping, the peer sends EAP-Initiate/Re-auth with the bootstrapping flag set to the home ER server, and may set the lifetime flag to ask for the rRK and rMSK lifetimes. The reply carries the local domain name if a DSRK was sent. If it has no Domain name TLV, the peer assumes there is no local ER server.

Replay protection uses a 16-bit sequence number kept per rIK, starting at zero. The server expects a number at or above the next expected value and then sets the expectation to the received number plus one. If the peer gets no reply it retransmits unchanged, but then MUST increment the sequence number for later messages. When the number wraps to zero, a full EAP authentication MUST be run. A server MAY accept a window of numbers so that several simultaneous ERP runs through different authenticators are not rejected.

Failures are reported by an EAP-Finish/Re-auth with the Result flag set to 1. If the cryptosuite was unacceptable, the server SHOULD include a list of acceptable ones (TLV type 5) and the peer SHOULD retry with one from it. Because a failure message could come from an attacker, the peer SHOULD keep going per its retransmission timers before giving up.
sections.eli5: Each message has a ticket number that only goes up, so a copied old ticket does not work. If the office says no, it may suggest a different kind of lock to try.

sections.title: The EAP-Initiate and EAP-Finish Messages
sections.content:
ERP adds two EAP codes: 5 (Initiate) and 6 (Finish). The Type field then says which message it is: Re-auth-Start (Type 1) or Re-auth (Type 2). A retransmitted EAP-Initiate keeps its Identifier, a new one uses a new Identifier, and the EAP-Finish Identifier MUST match the outstanding EAP-Initiate or the packet is silently discarded.

EAP-Initiate/Re-auth carries flags R (ignored), B (bootstrapping) and L (request key lifetimes), a 16-bit SEQ, TVs or TLVs, a Cryptosuite byte and an Authentication Tag covering the packet. EAP-Finish/Re-auth uses R as the Result flag (0 success, 1 failure). Exactly one keyName-NAI TLV must be present in each.

Attributes defined here: type 1 keyName-NAI, 2 rRK Lifetime, 3 rMSK Lifetime, 4 Domain name, 5 Cryptosuite list and 6 Authorization Indication. TLV types 128 to 191 are reserved for channel binding information. Cryptosuites are 1 (HMAC-SHA256-64), 2 (HMAC-SHA256-128) and 3 (HMAC-SHA256-256); HMAC-SHA256-128 is mandatory to implement and SHOULD be enabled by default.
sections.eli5: The messages are forms with a few fixed boxes at the top, such as a ticket number, and a stamp at the bottom that proves nobody changed the form on the way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC checks ERP against the AAA key management guidelines of RFC 4962. Keys are strong, fresh and limited in scope, and the rRK and rIK never leave the peer and server. Compromise of one rMSK, or of one authenticator, does not expose keys held by another. ERP gives mutual authentication of the peer and the server, but the algorithm choice is not a true negotiation because only one round trip is available.

Limits are stated plainly. There is no forward secrecy within ERP, so compromise of a DSRK retroactively compromises all ERP keys. Keys sent over AAA are exposed to AAA proxies along the way, so the AAA protocol is RECOMMENDED to be protected with IPsec or TLS. A cryptosuite list sent without an rIK is unprotected, so en route changes would go undetected.

A bogus EAP-Initiate/Re-auth could cause a failure reply. To avoid cutting off a working link, an ERP failure should not delete authorization state from a full EAP exchange. Multiple ERP runs under the same rIKname can be linked, which matters for privacy.
sections.eli5: The special keys never leave the two people who share them, and each room gets its own copy. If a thief gets the master secret, though, the old keys are in danger too.

sections.title: Lower Layers and Retransmission
sections.content:
ERP needs support from the layer beneath. The authenticator retransmits Re-auth-Start, but only a few times, since a peer without ERP silently drops them. The peer retransmits Re-auth, with a suggested maximum of 3 to 5 retransmissions over an unreliable lower layer. Over a reliable one, the timer SHOULD be set to infinite so no retransmission happens at the EAP layer.

If an authenticator gets a valid duplicate EAP-Initiate/Re-auth, it MUST resend its stored EAP-Finish/Re-auth without reprocessing it. The RFC recommends keeping that copy for 100 milliseconds.

Lower-layer specifications may need changes. IKEv2 must be updated to carry EAP codes above 4. Some EAP implementations treat such codes as errors instead of dropping them, so authenticators may be configured not to send Start messages, or lower layers may require a fallback to full EAP when ERP support cannot be verified. AAA transport of ERP messages is defined elsewhere, in RFC 5749 and a Diameter draft.
sections.eli5: If nobody answers your knock, you knock a few more times and then use the normal door. The office keeps its last answer for a moment so it can repeat it if you ask again.
